body_markdown:
Rare is the person who is comfortable with a three-on-the-tree column shifter. Even rarer are those who continue to clamor for them. Floor-shifted manuals, however, are deeply engrained in the driving experience of so many people that it hardly seems fair such handy mechanisms are mostly gone now. Certain enthusiast cars still offer them, which is great, but your run-of-the-mill econoboxes have all but dropped them in favor of CVTs, which is not great, because rowing your own gears in a base Corolla or Civic was always a reliable way to add a modicum of excitement to cars of that ilk. Which is not to disparage automatics, of course. Certainly there are a handful of great ones out there, too, which do their part to elevate the driving experience.


Hagerty Media staffers have driven some cars and shifted some gears, so this week we asked them to name the transmissions that stand out. You might agree with our choices, you might not, so give this a read and then let us know: What is the best transmission you’ve ever operated?


## Not That One Saab…


Sajeev prefers the sixer on a C6 Corvette ZR1.


Broad Arrow


This is a tough one for me, as I am not really that picky about transmissions. Automatics are generally better left overlooked, but they can be fun after installing a shift kit. Those days are gone, however, now that going into a menu on your dashboard lets you initiate a “Sport mode” that does basically the same thing. Meh!


All manuals are fun to me, except for one particular used Saab 9-3 I drove that had a shifter so inaccurate that it felt like a video game. My favorite, though, might just be the upgraded six-speed found in the C6 Corvette ZR1. — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Max Fun in a Mini


Kyle loved the way the shifter in his Mini John Cooper… Worked.


Kyle Smith


Although I love the TREMEC T56 I shoved into my 1985 Corvette during its engine swap, it is not my favorite transmission. Somehow—and this might simply be the rose-colored glasses of time—the top spot goes to the Getrag six-speed manual specced in the 2009 Mini Cooper John Cooper Works that served as my daily driver for a few years over a decade ago. The gearing was well spaced—I’m not talking about shifter throws here—and made it easy to keep the turbocharged inline-four in boost. I never found myself wanting for a “half gear” or cruising with the revs just a little higher or lower than the engine really wanted. That transmission helped make that car a delight to drive and likely played a part in me keeping it longer than I should have, but still not as long as I would have liked. — *Kyle Smith*


## Honda Engineering


Who knew the power of dreams was a six-speed?


[Chris Stark](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/chris-stark/)


The best shifter I’ve ever experienced was in a Honda S2000. I’m not alone in praising it, of course; everyone who has ever driven one appreciates how exact it feels in the hand. There are no linkages between the lever and the transmission that sap the feel, and the throws are short, quick and precise, with nothing vague about the process of getting from one gear to the next. It’s like flicking a light switch. The shifter is the perfect mechanical representation of what makes the S2000 so great. The entire machine is a precision instrument. — *Stefan Lombard*


## The One in My Daily


Eddy thinks the six-speed is Integra(l) to the Type S’s driving experience.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


This is like choosing a favorite food—it completely depends on my mood. I’d have to go for the shifter in my[Integra Type S](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/for-me-acuras-integra-type-s-makes-the-case-for-embracing-evolution/) as my all-around choice. Slick-feeling, low effort but crisp and precise, that car’s stick feels like a longer-throw S2000 shifter, and that’s a high compliment. On the other side of the spectrum is something like the Mustang Dark Horse’s TREMEC. It’s a high-effort affair (for stock, anyway) and feels as robust as the Integra’s is dainty. What the two shifters have in common is that they both convey the type of experience of the car they’re in while also being excellent tools.


Shoutout to old-school torque-converter automatics, though. With four (or fewer) gears, they might not always have been in the powerband, but they didn’t hunt for gears. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Isn’t It Obvious?


Steve’s answer is always Miata.


James Lipman


I’m not using much imagination here, but I gotta go[Miata](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/blue-streak-900-miles-home-in-a-freshly-bought-miata/) . When that car showed up in 1989, there were plenty of fun cars with manual transmissions, but the Miata’s manual and its little toy shifter almost started a new category of transmissions that are genuinely snickable on a winding road, easy to manipulate in rush-hour traffic, and feature gearing properly spaced to match the engine’s power—or help make up for it, maybe. That has continued right up through the current model year, a dependably consistent feature that proves there are people at Mazda in the design, engineering, and build process who understand and care about the Miata’s mission. It’s also idiot-resistant but not quite idiot-proof, as I demonstrated once in an MX-5 Cup race at Road Atlanta, when I aimed for fifth gear and found third, which severely disappointed the valve train. Screwing up on the Official Beginner Transmission for Motorsports cannot be explained away, and I’m a bit red-faced even now just writing about it. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## One of Each, Please


Ye olden ways…


Hagerty Marketplace/Heather-123


Just like an engine, a transmission should be evaluated based on its intended purpose. Some gearboxes are designed to be as maximally engaging, others to fade invisibly into the background. As such, I have a hard time picking just one transmission here. As for the manual, I’ll have to agree with contributor Jamie Kitman that the “rifle bolt” action of the four-speed manual in[an MGA 1600 Mk II](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/mg-at-100-storming-the-hudson-in-three-joyous-sports-cars/) is extraordinarily satisfying. He ranks the one in his ’62 just below a first-gen Miata’s five-speed, but the Brit box has a mechanical feel and vibration that can’t be beat, in my book.


… und der neue Stil.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


As for the automatic, the PDK (dual-clutch) used in Porsche’s 911 GT3 and Turbo cars (whether as a seven- or eight-speed) is about as bulletproof and versatile as it gets. Shifts are crisp and smooth around town, or rapid-fire when you’re racing around a road course, and the software programming is always spot-on. — *Eric Weiner*


## A Porsche… and a Ram to Tow It


The GT3’s manual shifter brings the noise.


Broad Arrow


I like my manuals to feel like a conductor’s baton—as if I’m manning an orchestra that demands precision but rewards with unforgettable noise. For that reason, I’m going to go with the six-speed manual out of the 2018 Porsche 911 GT3—in no small part because those six gears let loose 9000 rpm of flat-fix fury. That the shift action is precise and tight only elevates the feeling even further. You never feel like you are going to miss a shift, and you can choose to be rough on the thing—or lazily slot it up a gear without feeling as if you short-changed the car.


The ZF is perfectly suited to Ram trucks.


Ram Trucks


For an automatic, I’ve come to really love the ZF eight-speed in Ram pickups (and about 200 other Stellantis products). Truck transmissions are top of mind right now, as I’ve been in and out of the local shop trying to get the eight-speed in my 2016 GMC Sierra to behave, with limited success. That ZF in the Ram feels plenty proven at this point and every time I drive one, I’m pleased with the programming, the ratio spread, and just how well that box fits the pickup use case. — *Nathan Petroelje*
